speechtext:
1.	Having reference to question No. 18, answered May 7, referring to the sale of lots in Prince Rupert, owned by the National Railways, did the National Railways sell a large block of lots numbering upwards of one thousand about a year ago; if so, how many?

2.	Was the price at which these lots were sold $7 per lot; if not, what was the price?
3.	Were the said lots sold to a man named J. F. Duthie directly or indirectly; if not, to whom?
Hon. Mr, GRAHAM: The above questions were brought to the attention of Mr. Gerard Ruel, Vice-President and General Counsel, Canadian National Railways, at the meeting of the select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping on Tuesday, June 24, when Mr. Ruel made the following explanation of the transfer by the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company of the property in question:
The property in Prince Rupert was assessed at a very large assessment. We appealed against the assessment for a number of years with the intention of getting it reduced, but were unsuccessful. We did not consider the property of much greater value -rather a lesser value than the actual taxation- less than the assessment against it. We tried to give that property to the city, to have them take the property in discharge of the taxes. They said no, they would not do that; the taxes were assessed against the company, and we had no remedy, no redress. We said " Will you take the property and sell it to anybody to discharge the taxes?", and they said, " No, you have to pay the taxes." We, therefore, paid all the taxes, and then transferred the property to Duthie. If the city wants to get that property to-morrow, we will give it to them, we will get it back and hand it over to them, but we do not want to pay taxes on property that should not be assessed.
Mr. Ruel proceeded to explain to the committee that a conference of provincial treasurers was being arranged in order that a uniform basis of taxation of Canadian National Railways property rights might, if possible, be reached. At that conference the question of municipal taxation would also be considered. A. P. FORSTER

I have received from the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) the following statement:
I ask leave to move an adjournment of the House under rule 39, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely that the arrangements made by the post office authorities for the handling of His Majesty's mails are wholly inadequate and do not provide for the proper and sufficient delivery of mail matter.
Rule 39 paragraph (1) reads:
A motion to adjourn (except when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance), shall always be in order, but no second motion to the same effect shall be made until after some intermediate proceeding has been had.
Paragraph (c) of section (7) of the same rule states:
The motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session.
It is true that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) on the 17th June

Postal Employees
asked for leave to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the application or request of the postal employees. On reading that motion of the 17th June, one will see at once that it had reference to a strike to be, not a strike in existence. Since then the strike has taken place, and if I understand aright the purpose of the present motion, it is to discuss the arrangements consequent upon the strike. I call the attention of the House to section (4) of rule 39. Referring to the member who makes the motion it says:
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the House. If objection is taken, the Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and if more than twenty members rise accordingly, the Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.
Personally, I have some doubts as to the raison d'etre of the present motion; but comparing the two motions, that of the 17th June aaid the present one, I see that the motion of the 17th June has reference, as I have stated, to a strike about to take place, while the present motion refers to the postal arrangements .taken after the strike has occurred. Certainly it is a matter which is of grave importance but I have strong doubts as to its urgency, and for that reason I will ask the members who support the motion to rise in their places in order that I may see if the hon. gentleman shall have leave from the House to proceed with his motion.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I regret with every hon. member of the House that it is necessary to make this motion at the present time; I am sure that this necessity must be a matter of regret to hon. gentlemen in every section of the House. However, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that. I shall not detain the House very long. In view of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stated, I want to point out that we have already tried in every way possible to have the solution of the present difficulty hastened. We have asked questions and have received no answers; we have done all that we can possibly do, but without avail. There is an appropriate way in which this question can be brought up, and that is in the consideration of the estimates of the department. We have not had that opportunity. In connection with those estimates my right hon. friend the other day said that the Postmaster General, was still away, ill. That is true; but it is also true that we have an intolerable situation in this country just now. We have mail which is accumulating in vast quantities; we have a situation in which it is impossible for business men to carry on their affairs; we have a situation in which families are utterly unable to correspond one with the other. In Toronto we have a situation in which business is being retarded through a practically complete cessation of the postal service. It is true that there are a few letter carriers in service at the present time; there are a few in the business section of the city. But as far as the city generally is concerned it is not getting postal accommodation. Now this is a matter of very grave moment to the city of Toronto and to every one there who has anything to do with business. And the situation is not improving; my information to-day is that the mails are not moving. Speaking for myself, I may remark that I am unable to get my Toronto mail; I have been writing to members of my family in that city and have received no replies, and over the long distance telephone I learned that they have not been getting my letters, either. It is idle to say that the business of the country is being carried on as usual; it is not. This is a matter which this government ought to look into at the first possible opportunity; for after all it is only this government that can deal with it. I say therefore that it is the absolute and the immediate duty of the government to take steps to provide some remedy for the present state of things.
Let me point out to the Prime Minister that this strike, which undoubtedly we all
234i
deplore and which it is true we feel was very unnecessary, was after all not a "Red" strike; there are some first-rate men among the postal employees who have gone out. I admit that these men made a mistake; they were misguided in going out. But cannot something be done to-day to bring them back? If my right hon. friend took a trip to Toronto and visited the post office in West Toronto he would see there for himself an utterly impossible situation, where people are unable to get their mail. I am sure that the Prime Minister if he saw things in that city with his own eyes would be convinced that the present intolerable condition of things demands an immediate solution. I am not exaggerating the gravity of the situation for a moment when I say that, and I want to appeal to the government to take action without further delay. I am not going to delay the House any longer; I simply want to urge upon the Prime Minister and his colleagues the existence of an urgent responsibility which it is incumbent upon them to discharge immediately.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I think in fairness to the House I should make some comprehensive statement with respect to this matter. On June 18 and on previous days we noticed from press despatches that a strike vote was being taken throughout Canada, on the part of all postal workers in the country, against the adjustment of the Civil Service Commission's scale of salaries. I am not going to go at length into the details of the matter because I do not want to detain the House, but I want to state the main facts. On June 18 I was in consulation with the executive of the Postal Workers of Canada in this city and discussed very fully with them their difficulties, and their chief complaint was that the minimum wage as provided for under that schedule was not adequate and that the scale of wages did not run high enough. I want hon. gentlemen to remember that the scale demanded by the postal workers was very much higher than that granted by the Civil Service Commission. The executive of the postal workers made no intimation on that occasion that they would be willing to accept any lower scale. In fact I told them, and I think they agreed, that it was useless at that moment to discuss wages.
We did discuss some of the difficulties that they complained of most bitterly, the principal one being that a portion of the bonus which they had been in receipt of since April 1 would have to be refunded on the lower grade salaries if the scale set by the Civil Service
Postal Employees

Commission was to prevail. We agreed that no man should suffer by that reduction, but that we would immediately put into effect an order in council to provide that the bonus adjusted in 1924-25 would be continued until final adjustment of the whole matter, that is, at the point where the Civil Service Commission would have completed their duties and filed a new scale for the entire Civil Service. Not only that, but, as I mentioned in the House some days ago, the executive of the postal workers objected very strenuously because they did not have an opportunity to discuss all their difficulties with the Civil Service Commission in an intimate way-and I want to emphasize that expression,-in an intimate way. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I had some sympathy with that contention. They also asked that the law be amended so that their particular case would be taken out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission. I pointed out that there was no necessity for any amendment of the Civil Service Act, that, as has been stated so often in this House, it already provides a course for dealing with matters of this kind, in that although the Civil Service Commission has jurisdiction over the adjustment of salaries and conditions generally in the service, yet the government of the day must either approve any action taken by the commission, or refer the matter to parliament for final consideration. I told the men that the government were prepared to appoint a committee as soon as the final adjustment was made, and that committee would sit around a table with them and discuss all their grievances, and that if the report by that committee to the government was to the effect that an adjustment was needed, the government would take the responsibility of recommending to parliament such adjustment. Those were the two things outlined in a letter which was handed to the executive of the postal workers when they returned to Toronto.
In the midst of the discussions the Toronto workers went on strike. Perhaps it is only fair to say that before the executive came here they had already issued a strike order to go into effect at five o'clock the following day. They did endeavour to get a twenty-four hours' stay, and, generally speaking, that request was heeded by the service, except in the case of Toronto and Windsor and a few other towns throughout Ontario. There never was any strike in western Canada, or any cessation of work, and there was very little cessation of work in eastern Canada with the single exception of the city of Montreal.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is the history of the case up to date. I want again to say

what I said in the House on a former occasion, that in my opinion the Civil Service Commission is the proper body to deal with matters of this kind. Until their investigation is completed, I am not prepared to say definitely whether or not there are inequalities in the case of the postal workers which should be adjusted.
I will deal now with the strike itself. In the city of Toronto practically every man in the service, 1,600, walked out at 5 o'clock Wednesday evening, June 18. In the city of Montreal less than half the staff went out, scarcely 600 all told. The difference between Toronto and Montreal to-day is that in Montreal we have the nucleus of a trained staff to carry on business so that recruits can be taught much more quickly; but of course there is no such nucleus yet available in Toronto. As to Montreal, to-day mail is moving almost up to normal. Undoubtedly there will be difficulties for some time with a new staff hastily recruited and put to work under conditions such as prevail during a strike.
But in Toronto the situation is entirely different. The day after the strike took place we recruited 600 new men. There is no trouble in securing men for this work; there are more men offering themselves than we are able to take on, except in Windsor only, where there is apparently a disposition on the part of the citizens to back up the strikers in their attitude that their demands must be met before they return to work. I will deal with the Windsor situation in a moment or two because I think most hon. members will agree that I am not of a fighting disposition. In the city of Toronto up to the present moment, so far as I am aware, there has never been an offer from the leaders of the strikers to return to work; they insist that first of all their demands shall be met. They have insisted upon this from the start, and if the government must surrender to strikers, then those demands must be met. True, yesterday and to-day there is evidence that the strikers are not going to be so insistent.
With respect to moving the mail-and that is what my hon. friend dwells upon most- the government and the officials of the department have done everything in their power to move mail in the city of Toronto. What my hon. friend says is correct, there is a large amount of mail still undelivered, but we are sorting mail in this city in order to relieve congestion in Toronto, and we are delivering that to the large business and apartment houses in the centre of the city in bags for

Postal Employees
distribution by some individual in each building, and that distribution is going on throughout the central area of the city. It is true that in the outlying portions of the city we have not been able to reach business houses and manufacturers. But in the person of Mr. Lemon, the postmaster of Toronto, we have an excellent civil servant, a man who thoroughly understands his business, a man in whose hands we have placed the responsibility for the reorganization of this service, and a man who has shown that he is resourceful in meeting the tremendous odds and difficulties which handicap him at this time. These difficulties are indicated in a letter lying on my desk which I received a moment or two ago. It contains a report from substation E. It is pointed out that in that office there is a disposition on the part of the men who stayed on duty to delay delivery -which is what my hon. friend is complaining about-to hold up the public in line in order that they may be inconvenienced as much as possible in receiving their mail, although that mail is sorted and ready to be passed out through the wicket. I think the public ought to know this. I have no complaint to make about the police, I think they are rendering every assistance, but there are difficulties in places, and when you have a thousand strikers organized for the purpose of preventing delivery of mail, it is only natural to expect that they will do their best to create as much public inconvenience as possible.
As I say, no one wants trouble, and I am anxious to avoid it as much as possible. I hope that we shall soon be able to give a better service than we have so far been able to give. The key men, those who are the most valuable to the service, are the sorters in such large offices as that of Toronto. Every one of those men walked out, and it will take at least three or four raw recruits to do the work of one sorter who- is trained in his business. It takes days to teach a man to do that- work thoroughly. The trained sorter knows every street in the city; he can stand with a bundle of mail and sort it into the various bags for the different streets for delivery by the carriers, and he can do it much quicker than the man who does not know the city, who is not familiar with the streets, and who must proceed slowly in order to make a careful distribution of the mail. We are overcoming that difficulty as fast as we can. I am informed that Postmaster Lemon is recruiting a good staff, that he has obtained the services of men of intelligence and reasonable ability. I have no quarrel with the old staff; it was a splendid staff and very well organized. But they decided that they were going to take the law into their own hands and to proceed against the constituted authority of Canada, and by that decision they will have to abide. But it is my intention to give service and to give it as rapidly as possible. There will be inconvenience for some little time, but we now have almost 1,200 men recruited in Toronto. My hon. friend says there are men on delivery to-day. I question the advisability of starting a delivery before we have thoroughly organized the inside services; perhaps a delay of a day or two longer might have been advisable. But in his desire to restore the service as quickly as possible Postmaster Lemon has placed men out on delivery to-day, and I am willing to back him to the fullest extent in restoring the service in Toronto.
With reference to the strikers themselves, lest it be inferred that I have taken a position of intolerance with regard to theim I may say that I was visited yesterday by the mayor of Toronto and I gave him a copy of the letter forwarded to the strikers. I do not believe those men were advised of the full purport of the letter given to the executive; I do not believe it was fully explained to them. I thought it advisable to give a copy of the letter to the mayor. Three other gentlemen were here who represented themselves as members of a Liberal club-[DOT] Mr. Ross, Mr. Collins and Mr. Maguire. I gave those gentlemen copies of the letter, because 'they said they were in constant touch with the strikers and thought they could bring about a return to service of some of them. I noticed in the press this morning some statements that would indicate that again these men may not have been getting proper information, and again I hastened to get into communication with Postmaster Lemon and to tell him that my offer as made in the letter stood, and nothing else. We welcome everybody who will assist in a difficult situation like this, but I do not want it to be inferred that influence is being brought to bear in the matter by any section or any political party. Postmaster Lemon ,is in complete charge; he will remain in charge and will carry out the instructions contained in the letter which I delivered to the secretary of the strike committee when they left this city on Wednesday evening, June 18.

Now, let me first read a letter sent by the strikers to the Prime Minister-and I may say in this connection that the executive of the postal workers did not get into communication with the government from the day on which they received the schedule from the government until they wrote the letter, when they arrived in Ottawa on June 18th, that I am about to read. Here is the letter:
Dear Sir:
Acting on the wishes of the membership of the organizations concerned, as expressed in a Dominionwide ballot, a general strike in the postal service has been called to commence at five o'clock this afternoon.
It is regretted that the late hour at which this decision was arrived last night, and the necessity for ftiaste in entraining for Ottawa in response to a call from the government, made it impossible to convey this information to you sooner.
The necessity for the action taken is deplored by all our officers and members who trust that immediate favourable consideration by the government may yet enable us to assist in averting the move called for by the postal employees.
To that the following letter was given to Mr. J. E. Archer in reply, at about 3.10 in the afternoon. We had spent considerable time in consultation with the committee. I quote:
Mr. J. E. Archer,
Secretary, Canadian Federation of Postal Employees, Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,
This acknowledges receipt of a copy of your letter of even date addressed to the Right Honourable the Prime Minister advising him that:
[Mr. C. A. StewartJ
" Acting on the wishes of the membership of the organizations concerned, as expressed in a Dominionwide ballot, a general strike in the postal service has been called to commence at five o'clock this afternoon."
After discussion of this matter with the government, I am authorized to state that we regret the decision arrived at by your committee, and it is a matter of additional regret that your committee have not prior to this date officially indicated to the government your dissatisfaction with the recent salary revision for postal workers as authorized by the Civil Service Commission and the government.
Since the receipt of your letter of even date, a sub-committee of the cabinet has had the opportunity of discussing these matters at some length with your committee and have heard the views of your committee that further consideration should be given to the claims of the postal employees by the government.
In connection with this matter the Prime Minister in parliament yesterday stated as follows:
" We are prepared, when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries of the entire civil service, to consider that report carefully in the light of all the material which we have before us and to make to parliament, if we think it advisable so to do, recommendations supplementing those which are contained in the report of the Civil Service Commission. But we do not feel that we are in a position to make any recommendations to parliament at the present time with respect to the postal employees; and I hope that the employees of the Post Office department will see that the position which the government is taking is one which is in the interests of the entire civil service of the country and in the interests of the taxpayers as well."
We also in discussion of this date learned of the dissatisfaction of the postal employees due to the fact that in certain cases the present salary plus 1924 bonus was higher than certain rates proposed by the Civil Service Commission for the same class of employees; and I am authorized to state that in the case of employees whose revised rates, as determined by the Civil Service Commission are less than the former rate plus 1924-25 bonus, such bonus shall be continued until salary revision for the entire service has been consummated.
I am further authorized to say that in carrying out the plan and action proposed by the Prime Minister in the above quoted paragraph that the government policy is that when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries for the entire civil service, that opportunity will be given to the representatives of the employees in the postal department, or in other departments of the government who have objections to file against salary revision proposed by the commission to fully present their views to a sub-committee of the government, and to discuss such matters of differences as fully as may be necessary to ensure a thorough understanding, and it is hoped, a final and satisfactory agreement on the points in dispute.
I trust that your committee will at once take the necessary action to see that continuous operation of the postal service is maintained.

When a question is under debate no motion is received unless to amend it; to postpone it to a day certain; for the previous question; for reading the Orders of the Day.
That is exactly the case in the present instance. I quite agree that under ordinary circumstances a debate cannot be interrupted by another motion. But this is a privileged motion, and if the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) will read rule 36 carefully, he will find that this motion is receivable at any time and is not debatable nor amendable.

speechtext:

The House resumed from June 24 consideration in committee on Bill No. 47, to incorporate the United Church of Canada,-Mr. Forke -Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee has
under consideration section 2 and the amendment thereto moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown).

This bill has been, before the House since the 10th day of April. I had the honour and privilege of being a member of the Private Bills committee before which the bill in question was discussed, and I think I am saying nothing new when I observe that we are facing a very difficult problem in the consideration of this measure. Three churches in Canada, the Methodist church, the Congregational church and the Presbyterian church, appear before parliament and ask that legislation be passed to incorporate them into one body. We should have a very easy matter to settle if all of these three churches were unanimous in this request. Unfortunately, however, only two of them are unanimous; one of the three, the Presbyterian church, is very badly divided on the question. I need hardly refer to the great number of petitions and protests which have been submitted to parliament on behalf of those Presbyterians who do not hold that this union should be carried through. I believe that Bill No. 47 has attracted more attention in Canada than perhaps any other bill which has been before parliament in the last few years. The difficulty that now faces us exists largely within the

United Church of Canada
Presbyterian church itself; a grave dispute has arisen in that church, a large proportion of the members and adherents being apparently in favour of the proposed union while a large percentage have declared their objections to it. There appears to have been no way of settling the matter except by appeal to law. When a dispute arises over any question the logical conclusion is to try it in the courts; the courts are established for that purpose and in this particular instance I believe that no other course was open. It becomes more evident every day, at least to me, that the attempt on the part of the Presbyterian church, or of those who are in control of its affairs, to force that body into this amalgamation was an ill-timed one. I believe that the proper course would have been to let matters take their own logical course. But others thought differently and forced the issue, with the inevitable result that we are now faced with a tremendous split in the ranks of the Presbyterians.
It is not my intention to indulge in vain recriminations, because I do not think that any good purpose can be served in that way. We are faced I say, with this grievlous trouble; and the way to approach the matter if we hope to secure a settlement is certainly not by aggravating the situation and tiying to prove which side was right and which wrong. The discussion of this bill in the Private Bills committee has disclosed problems for which apparently no reasonable solution can be offered. No question can be settled, Mr. Chairman, unless it be settled right. I am confident that our friends the Methodists and the Congregationalists have no desire to force any unfair bargain on the Presbyterian church;
I believe that they want to do only that which is based on right. One of the principal objections raised in the Private Bills committee was that there would be no finality in the court proceedings which had been instituted, that they were likely to be prolonged, and were started merely for the purpose of delaying the union.
I purpose, Mr. Chairman, to move an amendment to provide for definite action in the shortest possible time. I believe that a judgment handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada will be accepted by all parties concerned. This is a sincere effort on my part to reduce the friction, bitterness and hostility which have grown up over the proposed union. The division in the membership of the Presbyterian church is in itself a tragedy. My only purpose in presenting this amendment is to secure a definite verdict to clear up the question of legal right, for when this question is settled I am sure it will do away with the 
present controversy which is so ruinous to the best interests of the whole church movement. I trust that the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) will find in this amendment common ground for a basis of settlement. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. MacLaren, in amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar:
The the amendment moved on June 24 by Mr. Brown that section 2 of bill No. 47, being an act incorporating the United Church of Canada, be amended by adding thereto the following words immediately after the words, "tenth day of December 1924":
"Provided that as respects the Presbyterian Church in Canada, the provisions of this act shall apply only when all doubt has been removed as to the power of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada under its constitution and rules to agree to a union of the Presbyterian Church in Canada with the Methodist and Congregational Churches upon the basis of union as set out in schedule A of this act: "Provided further, that this question shall be submitted for decision to the Supreme Court of Canada by a reference by the Minister of Justice."

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I submit that this amendment is out of order by reason of the fact that the necessary notice as required by rule 112 has not been given. This rule states:
No important amendment may be proposed to any private bill, in a committee of the whole House, or at the third reading of the bill, unless one day's notice of the same has been given.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the committee has not had the requisite one day's notice of this amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does any other hon.
member desire to speak on the point of order before a ruling is given by the Chair?

I desire to point out, Mr. Chairman, that Votes and Proceedings of yesterday contained notice of this amendment, and I submit that that is compliance with the rule quoted by the hon. member for Muskoka.

Mr. Chairman, I submitted this resolution in an endeavour to find a solution for the difficulty which confronts us. Although we have wrestled with this problem for three or four months, I regret to say we have not got very far along the lines of compromise. I was convinced that I had got something that would at least bring us together on common ground. I trust that mere technicalities will not be allowed 5 p.m. to upset this amendment, because, if so, we will be compelled to fall back upon the Duff amendment, which perhaps will not be altogether as acceptable and agreeable. I have no desire to utter any

United Church oj Canada
threat. I earnestly implore the committee to accept my amendment in the spirit in which it is offered as a sincere effort to effect a solution of the problem before us.
What is the essential difference between this amendment and the amendment of the hon. member for Lunenburg.
Time is the essence of the agreement.
How much time?
At least a year.

The hon. member for
Skeena (Mr. Stork) has implied that his amendment would probably lead to a solution of our difficulties; that is to say, that everybody would accept the bill as so amended. Have I correctly interpreted my hon. friend?

I think that the whole question before the court deals very largely with property rights. So far as I am concerned personally, I would accept the verdict of the court, whether it be for me or against me, because I believe in the kind of fight where the winner takes all.

My question practically
was whether the hon. gentleman is guaranteeing that the decision of the court, whatever it be, would be accepted by all parties concerned. He used the strong word "solution" in commending the probable success of his suggestion.

I rise to a Doint of order, Mr. Chairman. I understood that the Chair desired to hear hon. members is to whether the point of order raised by my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Hammell) was correct or not. My hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Putnam) is proceeding to discuss the merits of the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Undoubtedly the point or order to be dealt with is whether the notice of this amendment given in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday, and delivered to hon. members this morning, constitutes the one day's notice required by rule 112.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you make a ruling, may I direct the attention of the committee to the fact that only on the ground of a technicality at most would the amendment be ruled out? Should it be ruled out by your decision, the hon. member who presented it will not be prevented from moving the amendment at a later stage of the debate. As the Minister of National Defence has pointed out, notice does appear in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings, and a broad interpretation of that notice would indicate that the rules of the House have been complied with. This notice was given yesterday, and it appears in printed form in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday. If that time is not sufficient, certainly this amendment would be in order to-morrow, and I cannot see that the time of the House would be saved in any way by our taking up this amendment to-morrow instead of disposing of it immediately. As the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) has just pointed out, this amendment is more likely, in his opinion at all events, to bring the parties as near toge her as they can be brought in view of the u.ifortunate difference that exists between them. In any event it will serve to determine quickly the fate of the amendment and the clause now before the committee. All parties are anxious that a decision on this question be quickly reached, and I should hope therefore that the committee would agree to allow this amendment to stand. The only effect of my hon. friend's objection if sustained will be to have this debate continue for a longer time; it will not assist the argument one way or the other, while it may occasion a little more acrimony in discussion and, generally, serve no useful purpose. If we can in this matter, which is of great concern to all of us and to the country, take any step of a conciliatory character, one which will expedite a final settlement, I believe it is the will of the committee that we should do so.

I was looking in Beauchesne's book for the purpose of finding out whether there was any statutory definition of the word "day." The rule says that a day's notice of a resolution or amendment to a private bill shall be given. Now, in the record of the Votes and Procedings of yesterday, Wednesday, the 25th of June, there is contained a notice of this motion, and that, I submit,, is substantial compliance with the rule. The Votes and Proceedings, which record what was done yesterday, contain this notice, which was filed with the clerk the day before its proposed consideration by the committee. The night before last when we were discussing this question, I rose to a point of order which, I was then satisfied, as I ajn satisfied now, was a proper point to raise and should have been decided in accordance with my contention. As was suggested, however, we were dealing with a measure which the committee desired to consider in the broadest and fairest possible way to all parties concerned, and notwithstanding the fact that I was buttressed by authorities

United Church oj Canada
of the strongest kind, in deference to the suggestion of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Boys) I did not appeal from the decision of the Chairman to the whole House. I do not know what view you hold, Mr. Chairman, in regard to this matter, but I submit that for the Chairman to rule in accordance with a rigid compliance with -the rules would be to assume an attitude entirely diffrent from that which the Chair adapted two nights ago when we were dealing with the question I brought up, because upon 'a rigid interpretation of the rules and 'having regard to the authorities cited, the point was decisively ini my favour. In dealing with this question we must listen to any reasonable suggestion that is made by hon. members in good faith, having regard to the importance of the matter involved, touching as it does the interests bf a large proportion of the people of this country more intimately than 'any question I have known of in my parliamentary experience. I have not the least douibt that the rule has been substantially complied with, and I think it would be in the interests of the promoters of this bill if the hon. member (Mr. Hammell) would withdraw the objection he has raised.

I do not know very much
about the rules of the House, and I must say I am no stickler on rules. But this notice which has appeared in the Votes and Proceedings should not be considered a day's notice to hon. members. Speaking for myself, I never saw the notice, and I think the same would apply to the majority of members. It is a matter of some seriousness that hon. members should be asked to pass on an amendment of such great importance without having notice.
May I ask the Chairman when the copies of yesterday's Votes and Proceedings were placed on the files, yesterday or this morning?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know.

I may not be
quite in order, but may I ask when this debate is to be finished? I think the committee is ready to settle the question, and if we can come to some understanding as to this amendment I think we should do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Rule 40 of
the House, requiring two days' notice for certain classes of bills and motions, is as follows:
Two days' notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or address, for the appointment of any committee, or for the putting 
of a question; but this rule shall not apply to bills after their introduction, or to private bills, or to the times of meeting or adjournment of the House. Such notice shall be laid on the table before five o'clock, p.m., and -be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day.
I understand the custom has been that where the Clerk of the House has received notice in time to have it appear in the Votes and Proceedings of the day following, the two days' notice has reference to the appearance of the notice in the Votes and Proceedings of the day previously. Where one day's notice is required of amendments to private bills, the rule is:1	.
No important amendment may be proposed to any private bill in a committee of the whole House, or at the third reading of the bill, unless one day's notice of the same has been given.
I think, Mr. Chairman, the same interpretation should govern with respect to one day's notice. I understand that the Clerk of the House is quite prepared to state that he is following exactly the same practice with reference to the one day's notice in this regard as he follows with reference to the two days' notice in other cases.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Objection is made by
Mr. Hammell that the amendment moved by Mr. Stork is out of order under provisions of rule 112, which says:
No important amendment may be proposed to any private bill in a committee of the whole House, or at the third reading of the bill, unless one day's notice of the same has been given.
It seems to be agreed that this is an important amendment and therefore requires notice.
While it is true that Votes and Proceedings in question, number 77, bears yesterday's date it was delivered to hon. members in the regular course of events at about ten o'clock this day. The rule requiring notice for private bills puts those bills in a different position from that of any other bills, or resolutions or motions. Notice is required of this particular matter and the object of that notice is to permit publicity and prevent surprise. The Votes and Proceedings were delivered this morning, and the fact of whether or not notice of the amendment was sent in before five o'clock last evening cannot, I think, influence my decision in this matter. The day, notice is handed in, is considered the first day, the day the notice is printed the second day, and on the third day following the matter dealt with may be debated. I cannot bring myself to the view, notwithstanding the arguments which have been so well presented, that a notice of motion of an amendment to

United Church oj Canada
a private bill, filed with the Clerk last night, or at any rate before five o'clock, and delivered to the members on the morning of this day, is a sufficient notice under rule 112. For that reason I must rule that the amendment moved by the member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) is not in order. It has been said that if the debate continues the amendment will be in order. It would be, of course, operative to-morrow and on each subsequent day its regularity would be as strongly established, but I feel that I am acting according to the requirements of rule 112 to-day when I rule that the notice of motion in question is out of order. The debate therefore continues upon the amendment of Mr. Brown to section 2, and the hon. member for Swift Current has the floor.

As a member of the select standing committee on Private Bills and one who has been vitally interested in the subject that is being debated at the present time I wish to make my position plain. We have heard many views expressed by members of this House and by members of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, but it is not as a minister of that church that I wish to place my views on record. Of course I am not speaking ex-cathedra or exofficio but as a member of parliament.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has just stated that he was addressing this House as a minister of the church. He is therefore interested in this question.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the point of order is so highly technical that I have failed to grasp it.
The hon. member stated that he was not speaking as a minister.
In my opinion arguments for or against union-

I rise to a point of order. I think the point taken by the hon. member for Dorchester is absolutely correct. No hon. gentleman has the right to address the House as a minister of any denomination; he must address it as a member of this Chamber.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course an hon. gentleman must address this body as a member of the House, not as a minister of any particular denomination. I did not quite catch what the hon. member said and therefore do not entirely comprehend the objection raised by the hon. member for Dorchester.

The hon. member for
Swift Current stated explicitly that he was speaking as a member of this House not as a minister of the church.

The report in Hansard tomorrow will clearly indicate what I said. I made it quite plain that I was speaking as a member of this House.
Now, in my opinion the arguments for or against union do not or should not enter into this discussion. This is a religious prerogative over which no parliament under the British flag has any jurdisdiction. Moreover it is conceded by the chief counsel of those opposing the bill that those Presbyterians who wish to unite with the other bodies have a perfect right to do so. What they object to, is the taking of the whole Presbyterian church into organic union with the Methodist and Congregational churches while a considerable minority are opposed to it-and they have attacked the promoters of union on the following grounds:
1.	That the church has not the power to change its constitution.
2.	That it exceeded its constitutional authority in negotiating with the other churches with a view to organic union.
3.	That the bill would cause a violation of the church's trusts.
4.	That it destroys the doctrine of the church, the Westminister Confession of Faith.
5.	That it is clercial coercion.
These arguments have been advanced by various members and in divers ways, and it is my intention if possible to prove the falsity of their claims. Quite a number of speakers have suggested to the committee that it is not a wise thing to reverse the judgment of the standing committee. It has been claimed that the committee who listened to the arguments both for and against union is the best judge of the situation and they have quoted Bourmot and May in support of their argument. Now, I do not think that the argument presented in support of such a position is well founded, for the following reasons. In the first place, when any amendment is proposed to the preamble of a bill that has been accepted by parliament and sent to the select standing committee, it must be specially reported to the House, so that the members may know that such an amendment has been added. Why do the rules of the House demand that attention be drawn to the amendment, if it is not for the purpose of giving the committee the opportunity of rejecting or accepting an amendment that has been added to the bill? In the second place, it is well for this committee to know that

United Church of Canada
the. promoters of the bill do not agree to have this clause inserted in the preamble, and it was only inserted by a majority of the committee at an opportune time, when those opposed to the bill had a majority in committee. The same can be said of the section under discussion.	Anyone who reads the
original bill that passed the first reading in this House and was referred to the select standing committee, will know that it is entirely new, and was placed there in spite of the opposition of those who supported the measure. Under these circumstances, it seems to me to be one of those exceptional cases mentioned in Bourinot and May, and which was quoted at least twice during the course of this debate, by those opposed to the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). Therefore, in my opinion, this committee have a perfect right to reject this added section and to accept the proposed amendment that is before them.
Another argument advanced against the repealing of this clause is that the General Assembly is not the church; neither does it represent the people. Well, one might ask the question; "If it is not the church or the government of the church, and does not represent the people, what is it, and whom does it represent?" The people who are opposed to this bill, and who claim to be the stalwarts who champion the perpetuation of the Presbyterian Church in Canada by their arguments are striking at the very foundation of Presbyterianism. One member in his zeal for the church declared it clerical and official and ecclesiastical. Well, it might be well for such members to adhere a little more closely to that precious but much abused document, called The Westminster Confession of Faith. Let us see for a moment what this document says in regard to it. Section 31 of the Westminster Confession of Faith deals with the government and edification of the church. These assemblies are called synods and councils.
Section 3 reads as follows:
It belongeth to synods and councils ministerially to determine controversies of faith, and cases of conscience; to set down rules and directions for the better ordering of the public worship of God, and government to His church; to receive complaints in cases )f maladministration, and authoritatively to determine ,he same:	which decrees and determinations, if consonant to the word of God, are to be received with reverence and submission, not only for their agreement with the word, but also for the power whereby they are made, as being an ordinance of God, appointed thereunto in his word.
7 shall have occasion to refer to this question again when dealing with another argument which has been advanced against the

constitutionality of this bill, but for the present I am endeavouring to show to this committee that the assemblies and synods are peculiar to the Presbyterian form of government, and in the Westminster Confession of Faith have specific functions in regard to matters of faith and public worship. And, the conclusion reached by these same assemblies, if consonant with the Word1 of God, must be received with reverence and submission of the faithful.
So far, I have never yet heard the statement by my hon. friends and brethren that the union of the churches is inconsistent with the Word of God, and if this is not so, upon what ground do they attempt to oppose the union of the churches?
I, myself, as a Presbyterian minister was opposed to union during the early negotiating stages, but after the church had spoken with no uncertain sound through her courts, presbyteries, synods and assemblies, I acquiesced in the judgment of the majority, and as an obedient servant of the church and true to my vows at ordination, I could not conscientiously do otherwise.
The statement was made that: "If another vote was taken 75 per cent of the people would vote against it"; This is a mere guess and at least problematical, and the recent vote in the assembly does not bear out the argument.
It was further stated that the vote of 1916 is eight years old, and therefore, its value as a criterion of what the people want to-day is useless. Now, at the first glance this argument seems very plausible, but, on the other hand, I think it was clearly shown by Dr. Pidgeon in the committee that since that vote was taken, the church has proceeded just as fast as it was constitutionally possible for the Presbyterian church to do. I do not wish to 'take time to explain this, but let me say that a compromise was made at Winnipeg that the union question should be laid over until after the war and, when that time had elapsed, the assembly again took up the question of union and you are all familiar with the results.

My hon. friend stated
that formerly he was opposed to the union, and that when the judicial attitude of the church was for union, he as a follower of the church fell into line for union. Does he support this bill on his personal view of the merits of the bill or for the mere reason which he has advanced?

It must be remembered that this question has been before Canada for at

United Church of Canada
least twenty years, and my own experience as a missionary of the church goes back twenty years. In the early stages I was against it, as I admit, but in view of my experience as a missionary in the West I am heartily in favour of union. It has been stated by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that the personnel of the assembly is much the same. For some mysterious reason or other the commissioners chosen are always in favour of union. It may be true that a certain number of prominent members who are officials, are usually found at the assembly, but as regards the personnel of the assembly, seven-eighths of the commissioners are changed every year. Let me give this statement in regard to the vote of the General Assembly which met at Owen Sound in 1924.
Principal1 Fraser's motion approving the Duff amendment to the union bill was defeated by 444 to 92 in the assembly. Dr. Pidgeon's first motion was adopted by 427 to 96, and the names were recorded. Of the 523 voting 431 had not voted on union at the assemblies at Winnipeg in 1916, Toronto in 1921, or Port Arthur in 1923, where decisive votes on union were given and the names recorded.
In these four assemblies 2,094 votes were cast on union by 1,883 different persons as follows:

The percentage of duplication is less for those voting for union than for those voting against. Of the 1,672 votes for, 1,504, or 90 per cent, were given by different persons. Of the 422 against, 369, or S7i per cent were given by different persons. Two were privileged to vote at all four assemblies-a venerable leader of those opposing, and a missionary superintendent favouring union. The duplications are largest in the Presbyteries of Halifax, Montreal and Hamilton,
I think I have stated that the members of the assembly, in the four assemblies that have voted for church union, are not the same each year the vote is recorded. I think it is well for this committee, especially those who are not familiar with the Presbyterian system of government, and who perhaps belong to different churches, to weigh very carefully the appeals that are made by those who are opposed to the bill when they speak of the vote of the people. That people have be-235
come Presbyterians instead of belonging to some other denomination is due to the fact that they believe in the system of government which is peculiar to the church. Surely no member of this committee would seriously say that we must adopt another method or form of government, in order to pass this bill. To me, it is preposterous that any body of men should say that the church, through her courts, presbyteries, synods and assemblies has not the right to change or control the destiny of the church
What would the Anglicans and Roman Catholics say to a body of men, whether members of parliament or otherwise, who dictated to them in regard to the rules and regulations governing their church, or who declared, when a bill was brought before parliament that before it could pass its promoters must prove that it had a majority of the members of the church behind it and. on top of that, declaration, insisted that it should be sent to the courts?
How would you expect us to act if the situation was reversed? That is the question we have to consider, and if it can be proved that the church has acted constitutionally from the beginning to the time this bill came before parliament, I see no reason why this bill should not get the unanimous consent of this parliament.
The argument was raised by the chairman of the committee that the settlement of the union question is not for parliament but for the courts. I count the hon. member who was chairman as one of my most personal friends in this House, and his conduct during the very trying session was beyond reproach. I do not, however, agree with him, when he stated on Wednesday night that the matter of faith and doctrine was not for this parliament, but for the courts, to settle. I do not think the hon. member, on reflection, would repeat the statement. It surely is not for this parliament, or any parliament, or the Supreme court, or the Privy Council, to judge in matters of faith and doctrine. It is distinctly stated in the section which I read from the Westminster Confession of Faith that, the matter of faith and doctrine, as well as matters of conscience shall be settled, not by civil courts but by the courts of the church, and it is a privilege and prerogative that every church claims in Canada. Thus parliament to my way of thinking would be very unwise to force such an issue in the courts at the present time.

When that statement was made by one of the leaders of the church, it could not help causing indignation in the breast of everybody that was at that meeting, because if it is modernism, for men who take a vow to uphold the doctrines of the church into which they were ordained, to come before a committee and ridicule and, for other reasons, make light of their vow, then I prefer to stand by the religion that I was taught at my mother's knee rather than to follow the leaders of the Presbyterian church who appeared before the Private Bills committee.
It is said that a minority in the Presbyterian church is opposed to union. We do not agree that such is the case, but for the sake

I looked up the records of the Congregational church, and so far as I can obtain them, there are about 32,000 members. Yet their rights are to be protected, and rightly so, in going into this union; but those that form the so-called minority are much greater in numbers, and I do not think any one would gainsay that the Presbyterians in the Dominion of Canada far outnumber those who belong tc the Congregational church.
I maintain that the minority has its rights, and you cannot force anyone into a church to which he does not wish to belong. To-day I happen to be a Protestant. Why? Similarly, I happen to be a Presbyterian beoause my people were Presbyterians and largely because I was taught the doctrines of the Presbyterian church. I do not deny that right to anyone and I demand the same right for myself; and I defy any church court, any legislature or any parliament or individual to take it from me. It cannot be done. You may pass all the laws you like but you can never take away my liberty of conscience. I owe that to no earthly potentate.
I saw in a newspaper this description of a meeting:

We have heard a good deal since this debate began about the rights of the minority and doing justice by the minority, and it comes from our Presbyterian brethren. The rule of that church as that the majority govern, that I think is the rule in every Protestant church, and the rule is absolutely necessary to the continuance of any Protestant church. Otherwise, what have we? If the minority can impose its will upon the majority, what will be the result? Why, we may have half a dozen or a dozen minorities and each one will be ruling the roost. The only method by which a Protestant church can survive is for the majority to rule. When a man becomes a member of the Presbyterian church, he does so voluntarily. He does not acquire any property right in that organization. It is not like going into a business enterprise. The arrangement is purely voluntary on his part. He continues his membership and he retires when he sees fit. He is accepted if they see fit to take him. He is expelled if he does not behave himself according to the rules and regulations. The whole arrangement is an association at will. As I have said, he has no rights in the property. When he retires he takes none of it with him and, therefore, I say that he is merely there subject to the rules of that church.
