We cannot take any.

There is no voice and no court to which we can appeal for an opinion, if it be not the court set up by the members of the Methodist church itself. This parliament did not set up that court, it had no right to set it up; but within the jurisdiction of the Methodist church itself has been created a tribunal called the General Conference. That General Conference, in the name of the Methodist church of Canada as its official mouthpiece, said "We want to go into this union". Can we go behind that, even though a number of Methodists said they did not want to go in? It is for the churches themselves to reorganize their own organization and get a proper mouthpiece to express their views, if they have not got it at the present time. The Congregationalists have the same method to which I will not allude, because I am not as familiar with it.
We are in a very grave and responsible position to my mind.	We are not here
voting as unionists or anti-unionists, we are here to adhere to the prerogatives of parliament and not to encroach on the prerogatives of the churches. These churches have said, through the only organizations that we as a parliament know of; through the organizations that they have erected, constructed and maintained themselves from time immemorial, that they desire this union. We are here to ask ourselves, should vve allow these three great churches to carry out their own expressed wish, or are we as a parliament to interfere and place a barrier in the way to prevent those churches doing what they have asked us to allow them to do? If it had not been essential to have legislation here, these three churches would have been united, and we are only an incident in the machinery provided to allow this union to take place. I say it is a difficult situation. Perhaps I should not say that, but it is an important moment, not only in the history of the churches, but it is an important moment with reference to the constitution of our parliament and the definition of its rights. If we are going to take the position that we can legislate to encroach upon the rights which we in Canada have given to the various churches, and which is one of the bulwarks of our freedom in this country, then we are taking a new stand and we are taking the position that we have the right to create a state church in the Dominion of Canada.

I have not said whether I am in favour of union or not but I do maintain-and this is the only position I take-that as a member of parliament it is my duty, I believe, to respect the rights of the Presbyterian the Methodist and the Congregational bodies in this country, and they, through their courts instituted by themselves, have decided that it would be a good thing for the great cause which they represent that they should be united in their efforts instead of being divided. I believe I am doing my duty as a member of parliament by keeping myself aloof from the differences between the churches and saying to these churches:	I am prepared
to support you in carrying to a consummation through this bill, the objects for which for years you have striven, and which in your considered judgment are best for the churches and best for humanity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the
vote is taken, may I say a word with respect to the attitude of the government and my own attitude on this important measure?
It is hardly necessary again to draw the attention of the committee to the circumstance that this bill is in no sense a government measure. It is a private bill introduced in this House by one of its most respected members, at the instance of the governing authorities of three great churches that have asked for the right to be united into one church. Prior to the present moment, only two members of the government have spoken, and each of them, I think, has spoken emphatically. They have not been on the same side in the controversy. When the division comes later in the evening, I have no doubt hon. members will see that the government itself is very much divided on this question. I should like to make this clear, because throughout the discussion of the last month it has come to roe that rumours were being circulated that 1 was taking a certain attitude and requesting members of my party to adopt likewise a similar attitude. At other times, rumours have come that my attitude being otherwise, the difference of view expressed by some members of the parly was due to that different attitude. I wish to make it perfectly clear, that in this matter, from the beginning of the discussion until this moment, I have not desired that any member of parliament and particularly any member on this side of this House should in this matter vote other than as his conscience and sense of duty and right impel him to vote. I cannot make it too clear that the government as a government is assuming no attitude in this matter.

United Church oj Canada
has no responsibility for the outcome; and tnat as I speak here to-night I am voicing my opinion only as one member of this House, and on this question I wish to express that opinion with the utmost humility.
May I say first of all that the bill having come to the House in the manner described too first question we are obliged to ask ourselves is:	Is the purpose one which commends itself to parliament? The object of union of churches, the incorporation of churches for the purpose of union, is a great purpose, and if incorporation is needed to give effect to that purpose, I think all hon. members will agree that in accordance with what is legal and right we should further that object in so far as it is possible for this parliament so to do.
We have next to ask ourselves the question: Has this parliament jurisdiction in this matter? And have the churches that are applying to this parliament for incorporation jurisdiction or power to consummate the union which they have asked this parliament to give effect to by the bill which is before us? Having considered these points, we have also to ask ourselves: Have the churches complied with their own constitutions and established procedure in the steps they have taken to effect union; and, in the bill which we have before us, has due regard been had for the interests of minorities that may be affected? As to the last question, whether the riglhts ofi minoritiesi have been safeguarded, we can deal with that when we come to the sections of the bill in reference thereto. I think it will be found that if in other particulars the bill is satisfactory, those who have had to do with the measure, have endeavoured to consider in a broad and generous way, the rights of minorities. As to the question of compliance with procedure in seeking union, as nearly as I can gather, there is pretty general agreement, that' the procedure so far as it relates to matters other than the power of the Presbyterian church to ask for union, or rather to form the union contemplated, has been regular and in accordance with the constitution and polity of the respective churches.
As to jurisdiction, it is important that the interested parties not less than parliament should understand clearly that, under the British North America Act, certain rights of exclusive jurisdiction are assigned to the provinces; others are assigned to the federal parliament. The well known section of the 237
British North America Act, section 92, under the heading of the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures, reads as follows:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say.
Then follows an enumeration of the classes of subjects and number 13 is "property and civil rights in the province." Therefore, this federal parliament has no power whatever to legislate in regard to any matters concerning property and civil rights within the different provinces. This bill necessarily concerns property and civil rights in many particulars, and I think it is important, we should make it perfectly clear, in any legislation that may be passed, albeit such a clause be but declaratory, that in the provisions of this measure, this parliament is not going beyond the scope of its jurisdiction in any particular. I have, as possibly hon. members may have noticed, drafted an amendment which I think will be sufficient to cover that point and which I believe the House will accept without question when we come to the later stages of the bill.
As to the one remaining point, the power of the churches to effect the consummation of union, from what I have heard and read of the committee's proceedings, from what I have gathered in communications that have come to me, not by tens or hundreds, but I might say almost by thousands from all parts of this country, and from what I have gathered from the discussion in this House during the course of this debate, I believe there are two extreme positions, neither of which is deserving of support. There is one extreme which maintains that, under no circumstances, under no conditions, should union of these three churches be permitted. There are those who as respects one of the churches concerned take the position that its constitution concerning principles is such that its members, those in authority, have not the right to effect a union with the other two churches. They say that that is a condition that cannot be changed. Let me be quite plain. That question has not arisen with respect to the Methodist church nor with respect to the Congregational church. It has arisen with respect to the Presbyterian church. There are some who take the position that the Presbyterian church, even by the will of the authorities duly constituted, has not the power to ask foi union, to form a union with the other two churches. Those who support that point of view seem for the most part to be unwilling to permit that question

United, Church of Canada

to be decided except in the courts, and as the result of litigation which, to appearances, might extend over a number of years.
Personally I have little sympathy with such a point of view. Personally, I do not see why it should not without litigation be possible to decide whether or not that power exists in the Presbyterian church. If such a power does not exist, I cannot see why, knowing the nature of the disability, unless it be of a character which commends itself to parliament, a means should not be found by parliament of speedily removing that disability. That is the reason why, having regard to what is customary in such references, much to my regret, I find it difficult, indeed impossible, to support the amendment which has been made to the original bill by the committee of this House to which it has been referred. That amendment provides that this question must be settled by carrying a particular case, which is in the courts at the present time, through the Supreme court and if need be, to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council; and by mentioning the first of July, 1926 as a possible date at which parliament might deal with the question again suggests a period of litigation seemingly interminable. Who is there in this House this evening who can believe it to be in the interests either of church or state that a great religious controversy should be carried on in this country for the next three, four or five years? I think such a controversy would oe the greatest misfortune for our national life, and certainly a very grave misfortune, for the religious life of the churches concerned; and for my part I am not willing to support any proposed legislation which contemplates litigation over a term of years. I think the gentlemen who in the name of their churches asked us to enact this measure are right in the position they take in regard to the amendment suggested by the committee, not so much on the ground of principle, as on the matter of time and the amount of litigation involved in what it proposes. They say, "We came to you for legislation and you are giving us litigation." I do not think we should give litigation. I think we should find means of settling this controversial point without the necessity of prolonging controversy in the courts.
What is the other extreme position? At the other extreme you have a number of gentlemen who say, "We wish to have this union consummated, and we ask the parliament of Canada to consummate it whether

or not the Presbyterian church has the power to form a union with the other two churches." They ask us to use the might of parliament- because parliament, they contend, is all powerful-to consummate the union irrespective altogether of whether the Presbyterian church as at present constituted has the power to form such a union with the other churches. They ask us to compel the Presbyterian church to enter that union. Now, speaking again in all humility, may I say that such a method of proceeding does not appeal to me at any time; and it appeals to me less with respect to matters concerning the Christian religion and the Christian faith than in regard to anything else. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Raymond) last night, speaking in this House, said very truly and wisely that the more of power we have the more careful we should be in the manner in which we exercise it; and when I am asked to use the might of parliament, regardless altogether of whether the power does or does not exist in the Presbyterian church to unite with the other churches, to compel that great historic institution, while a large proportion of its following say and believe the church has not the power, to go into union with the two other bodies, I for one cannot see my way to support such a method of proceeding.
May I draw the attention of the House to this circumstance. The Presbyterian Church in Canada has suffered disruption through this controversy. Let us remember that this great church is split in twain; its membership is irrevocably divided; never again will there be in this country the one Prebyterian church which our fathers and our forefathers have known in this Dominion. We are standing at the parting of the ways and we can help to bind the wounds that have been inflicted in this process of disruption, or by our action to-night we can help to make more difficult for all time the position not only of those who stay out of the union but also of those who go in. It is a time for conciliation not coercion. There are hundreds and thousands of men and women- in the Presbyterian church who want to go into the union; but do they want to enter the union in virtue of a power which their church does not possess or concerning the possession of which there can be a shadow of doubt? Does the Methodist church, does the Congregational church, do the Presbyterians who desire union, wish to found their new church upon a doubt, not to use a stronger term? Is that to be the foundation for a great church propagating the teachings of Christ-a foundation of

United Church oj Canada
doubt? Or is it rather the desire and the aim of all who seek to carry out the teachings of the Master that whatever they do shall be done in a spirit of conciliation and goodwill and in a manner which, if such can be found, will remove all doubts whatsoever?
You ask me, how are these two extreme positions to be reconciled? That is the problem. I do not believe it is difficult of solution, certainly not in a Christian spirit; I believe the solution will be found in a practical application of the central tenet of the Christian religion, following what is known to us as the Golden Rule, to do unto others as we would have them do unto us. I believe that the Methodist church in this country and the Congregational church both wish that rule to be observed; I believe that the Presbyterians are anxious to see it applied in this instance in a solution of this question. Personally it is the only rule I wish to be guided by in reaching a decision as to my attitude on this matter; and it is because I wish to govern my own thought and action in accordance with that rule that I regret that this afternoon the amendment which was proposed by my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Stork) was not permitted by common consent of the committee to be moved and to be put before us for the purposes of debate. I believe that the amendment which that hon. gentleman offered provides a way out, a way which should be satisfactory to all who really desire the consummation of union on a foundation that will be enduring and above criticism in any regard. What was his proposed amendment? It was that this bill should become law. He accepts the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar that the bill should go into force in July of next year; he accepts that. But he adds one proviso, namely, that as respects the Presbyterian church the question of the power of that church - to unite with the others, which is the only matter in doubt, shall be settled by a reference by the Minister of Justice of a stated case to the Supreme court.
Who outside of the Presbyterian church can determine that power?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Members of
the Presbyterian church say to-day that there is a doubt as to whether that power exists; some of those who wish the union admit that there is that doubt. Those who are opposed to union say that their opposition is founded on that doubt, most of those who are asking for the union are as emphatic in their view that the Presbyterian church has the neces^ sary power as the opponents of union are in 237J
the view that with the church as constituted, it does not exist. If those who are favourable to union are confident in this 'belief, what is there for them to fear from a reference of that particular subject to any tribunal?

In the event of the Presbyterian church going to the courts, and the 'courts deciding against the General Assembly having power to go into this union, we would (have two churches united. What would ,happen to the third?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad my (hon. friend has asked that question, for now [I know what is in his mind, and it is one of the points which if I can I should like to make clear.
The suggestion of the amendment-and it would have been my own suggestion to the committee had it not found its place in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday- is that this House refer this particular question, which is the only matter in doubt, by means of a stated case to the Supreme court. That case can be submitted to the Supreme court and finally determined before the end of the present year. Assume it iis settled as the unionists say, or believe, that it will be settled; that it is determined jthat the Presbyterian church has the necessary power, then this entire bill becomes operative and no one, whether anti-unionist or unionist, can reasonably cherish ill-will towards his fellows as a result of the conclusion which has been reached. Some tribunal sooner or later has to decide the question, and if .parliament refers this matter to the Supreme court for decision, it is simply prescribing the method that by and large has to be taken .in all great controversies-that of ultimately .referring to arbitration disputes that cannot ,be otherwise settled. If you object to the Supreme court, for my part I wouid not .mind whether the tribunal was in the nature .of a specially constituted commission of judges or lawyers or any other class of persons to be agreed upon. As I have already said, if such a tribunal were to decide that the church has the power which is now in doubt, the legislation would become effective and the union would be consummated in a manner to which no one could take exception.
But suppose the tribunal were to decide that the church has not the requisite power, what then? It will have to give reasons for so deciding. We will then know, the church will then know, the country will then know, what those reasons are. Is it because of some doctrine fundamental or otherwise of the Presbyterian church that union is impossible?
United Church of Canada

Is it because of some rule of organization that union with other churches is impossible? We will know what it is, and knowing, parliament will be in a position to act. If it is a disability of a character that should be removed, all that has to be done is for Presbyterians who desire union to come to parliament and ask that such disability be removed. Does any hon. member of this House believe that if parliament were asked to remove a disability which did not commend itself to the judgment of parliament and which prevented a great church, after following its regular methods of procedure and complying with its duly constituted rules, from participating in a union with other churches, that parliament would refuse so to act?
I hold the view, Mr. Cha.rman, with respect to matters of church and state, that the church within its sphere has powers and jurisdiction just as complete with respect to its doctrine, polity and destiny as the state has with respect to its own constitution and destiny. I would never support interference by the state with the right of any church to determine its own destiny, to shape its own polity, to do what it wishes with respect to its own doctrine. I know there are many who will not agree with me in that, but I believe that this House would be prepared were it shown wherein the Presbyterian church cannot control its own destiny, shape its own polity, and do as it will with respect to its own doctrine, to come to its relief and unless the reasons to the contrary were unanswerable would give it the fullest powers possible, and do so in a manner which would remove altogether any possibility of further doubt in this regard. Then the Presbyterian church, under the legislation which is already on the statutes, would go into this union not in an atmosphere of doubt and uncertainty but as a matter of fully established and recognized right.
Now, have I answered the question which my hon. friend wishes to ask?

I cannot say that it is answered satisfactorily. Provided the decision went against the Presbyterian church, then we would have the Methodist and Congregational churches united-something which was never intended by the church courts.
Why not?

It would not be legal. They have no authority to enter into any engagement of that kind. Their engagement is for the uniting of all three churches, and the courts deciding against the Presbyterian church,

we would have to come back to parliament, and parliament would be still forcing upon us the very same thing we are objecting to tonight.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We would be in a very different position. What we are being asked to do to-night by those who wish church union under this legislation is to declare that that union shall be formed whether or not the Presbyterian church has power to enter into it.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We cannot get away from that. We are being asked to compel that union whether the Presbyterian church has the power to enter into it or not. Now, inside of two or three months we can settle whether or not the Presbyterian church has that power. If it is found that the
12	m. Presbyterian church has not that power, and the majority of its members want that power given to their church, and ask this parliament for it, I believe parliament will be prepared to give the necessary powers to form a union. Then the union can be formed in accordance with legal rights and be in every particular above doubt and suspicion.
With respect above all else to the foundations of a new and great church, it seems to me that we shall be serving the interests of all concerned, if we take care to see that the church is formed on a secure foundation, a foundation that is beyond any question of doubt, a foundation that can give rise to no questionings or misgivings on the part of its membership, or to recriminations on the part of those who have not become of its membership.
In conclusion, may I remind this House that next to the sacred association-

Before my right hon. friend concludes his address, may I present my question regarding a stated case? How is he going to prepare a stated case in which the facts are at issue and which involve questions of doctrine and origin? Stated cases are prepared when the questions at issue are readily agreed upon.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am informed on what I believe to be as good legal advice as one can obtain that it is possible to form and submit a stated case in this matter.
Who would do it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Under the
amendment which has been moved by the

United Church oj Canada
member for Skeena, the burden of having the case prepared would rest upon the Department of Justice, and I should be prepared to advocate that the government bear the total expense of having this particular matter settled in that way. What I am aiming at in the point of view I am suggesting to the committee is to find some way of quickly and effectively resolving any doubt. Having resolved the doubt one way or the other, union can then be made possible in a legal way and in a manner which will leave no room for criticism or heart burning after union has been effected.
Would that decision require subsequent legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the decision is in favour of the unionists, the legislation which we are passing now settles everything. If it goes the other way, then wrhat will be necessary will be for the duly constituted1 authorities of the Presbyterian church who feel they are being hampered in the matter of union through some disability that has been discovered, to come to parliament and ask that the disability be removed. Unless the disability prove of a character which parliament should not remove parliament may be expected to act favourably upon such a request and when parliament has removed the disability then they will come into the union, and the new church is formed in a regular and unimpeachable way.

The Prime Minister has
alluded to the necessity of referring a stated case to the Supreme court. There might be some doubt, he said, with respect ti the right of the Presbyterian church to change its doctrine and consummate union. Does he want us to take him seriously when he contends that the people of Canada would accept the judgment of a civil court in matters respecting doctrine?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the proposed reference to the Supreme court does not appeal to my hon. friend's judgment, I have already said that I should be glad to have suggested any other commission, any other tribunal, a commission of any character to be agreed upon, to which this question of doubt might be referred and settled. Let that body whatever it may be by deciding the nature of the disability give a decision which will guide parliament. Surely if we want to find a way out that will help to reconcile differences it can be found in that way
Next to the sacred associations of home, the most sacred associations in the lives of men -to some perhaps more sacred even than those of home itself-are the associations of the Christian church. This parliament cannot afford to be indifferent to the feelings entertained by hundreds of thousands of men and women throughout this country with respect to the attitude of parliament toward their church. At all times parliament has to be prepared to recognize great bodies of opinion. What about the group of hon. gentlemen opposite, led by the hon. member who introduced this bill (Mr. Forke)? They represent a great interest in this country, and we hear them continually speaking of the need of the nation, whilst legislating for others, to consider their special interests. What about my friends at the far end of the chamber opposite? They speak about the interests of labor, another class, another group. All through our national life we recognize that whether or not we see eye to eye with the different groups that go to make up this great nation, we are nevertheless bound to respect the feelings and the beliefs and the convictions of the great bodies who constitute minorities. In the Presbyterian church there is from one end of Canada to the other, a great body of earnest and God-fearing men and women who feel very deeply in this matter. They may be a majority, they may be a minority. If we can help, as I have said, to remove from their minds the feeling that their church is being torn asunder and substitute for it a feeling that whatever division is now inevitable is being made in accordance with what is reasonable and right and in accordance with the best traditions of parliament, then we will be rendering a great service not only to the parties interested in the consummation of this important union, but also to our country as a whole.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The nature of the
question under review to-night is such as has never in my time been before parliament. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is only expressing appreciation of the real position when he says that there are wide differences of view, sunderings of sentiment, and that on both sides of a great controversy are ranged some of the very best people of our country. Of course we all inspect the views of those who differ from us, and we must carry that respect to even greater lengths and depths in relation to a question such as now agitates us all. I regret exceedingly that any words have been uttered
United Church of Canada

impugning the high motives or the personal conduct of any connected with either side of the controversy. For myself I am in disagreement with very many of the best friends I have. My inclinations lead me naturally to cling to the church with which my family for many generations has been associated. Personal ties bind me closely to those, both in this House and throughout the country, who seek earnestly, even passionately, to maintain in its present status the church of our fathers. But I must say very frankly that after the closest thought I have been able to give to the subject I find the line of reason leading me the other way. I feel bound to state, at once, so that there may be no misapprehension, that in my judgment the duty of parliament is to pass this bill and that parliament cannot usefully evade that duty by any amendment either such as is suggested by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), supported by the Prime Minister, or that sponsored by the hon. member for Lunenberg (Mr. Duff), and now embodied in the bill.
This is one of those questions which require the most careful reasoning; where confusion of thought is not only possible, but almost inevitable; where men are easily driven from the straight path of logic by sentiments which are powerful and by passions which are deep. I do not claim to be in the least exempt from these influences myself; I only endeavour to dispel them to the best of my power and to get at what I feel we ought to do by as simple and careful a route as I can find. In what I say to-night I am not expressing my views with any idea of changin' those of others; indeed, so firm have convictions been rooted that I could not hope to do so. The most I aspire to accomplish is briefly and simply to lay down the considerations which guide me, in the hope that in the future, when the result of our action now shall be reaped in all its fruits, these reasons may be looked back upon as adequate and appropriate.
We have a bill before us 'the purpose of Much is, as I express it, to confirm the union of three great denominations of religion- the Presbyterian church, the Methodist church and the Congregational church. I find myself in agreement with the argument presented to-night in very clear and forcible form by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). I do not think he fully explored the question, but to the extent that >he did I find myself unable to diverge from his line of thought. These three churches come to parliament, having expressed their will through those tribunals which alone

are empowered to express their will. Not only have they expressed it to us, but they have taken action upon it themselves. To the utmost of their power they have formed a union-indeed they have consummated the union-buit, as all agree, legislation is necessary because of the civil rights involved, because of properties over which in some cases the legislatures and in other cases the federal parliament have jurisdiction, and because of the necessity of bringing those properties and the corporations which control them into conformity with a new relation created by the union.
Those appealing for the legislation say: " The question of union or non-union is ours, it is not yours. It is a matter for the exercise of our rights within our spheres. All we call upon parliament to do is to consummate our action because of the necessity involved in the existence of these properties, and as well, because of the desirability of putting into corporate form the union so effected." The Minister of Railways argues that these bodies have expressed their will through their definitely constituted authorities, their courts. No one disputes that to the extent to which those courts could accomplish their end they have acted in proper form. That is to say, if we admit that they had power to do what they have done they have gone about it through the proper route; they have taken all the precautions; they have paid heed to all the safeguards, and expressed the will of their churches as best they could. They come to parliament then and claim that we have no right to deny them the consummation of the union which they themselves have effected.
It is contended on the other side that one of those churches, namely, the Presbyterian, has exceeded its powers in taking those steps essential to the union. It is curious enough to reflect that no such contention is levelled as respects either of the other denominations-the Methodist or the Congregational-and the reason given is because there is no dispute, no great division of opinion in those two denominations. But does that reason really dispose ol the question? If the power to unite did not exist in the one I, as yet, have never found any reason to conclude that it did exist in any of them. I have not found in what investigation I have made any possible disability affecting the Presbyterian church, which did not equally affect the Methodist and the Congregational church. If it appertained to one, it appertained to the others and merely because it has not been drawn

United Church of Canada
attention to by the supporters of those others would not prove that parliament should be troubled about the matter in the one case and utterly ignore it in the case of the rest.
In this discussion the general expression has been that this church-the Presbyterian church-has not had the power to take those steps necessary for union. I do not know whether those using this expression intend always to say that the General Assembly of the church did not have the power delegated from the church itself to take those steps. Usually those who argue on the question of power contend that the assembly never received from the church itself-I suppose the people of the church-the power to take the action which it did take. There is some difference between that and arguing that the people could not give to the assembly the power to take the action. Personally I am of the view that not only had the church the inherent power but that the church had delegated such power to the assembly. But as I proceed to discuss very briefly this point and buttress my opinion I ask hon. gentlemen to remember that I do not rest my support of the bill on the foundation of this opinion. Others may have just as good and as strong a feeling the other way. I will contend later that it does not matter which is correct, the bill cught to pass, but I do take the view that the church inherently has the power and, as well, that it has expressed the authority and created the court by which the power may be exercised.
What after all is this power of union? Does it consist in anything more or less than the power to change doctrine? I ask most earnestly hon. gentlemen to reflect on that sentence. Does the power to unite really embrace anything more than the power to alter doctrine, to modify doctrine? If the power to modify doctrine is conceded what is there between that and the power to unite with any other church holding the doctrine so modified? I say, once the church is conceded power to modify doctrine we have ended the discussion as far as the power of union is concerned.
Mr. MaeLAREN: May it not be that one can change a doctrine to a limited extent, not being a fundamental or a radical change? No one questions the right to make minor changes, but I ask the right hon. leader if he asserts that it is possible for every General Assembly to change fundamentally while there is a basis of doctrine that is accepted by the church?

What is in the mind of
the hon. gentleman is not a question of the power of the church itself to change fundamentally but whether there is a power in the assembly to change fundamentally. I will discuss that, and while I know I cannot convince my hon. friend, whose views I respect profoundly, I will explain why I am convinced myself. I think the power to change is inherent in the church and that the assembly has the power delegated to it to express the will of the church in this regard, and that there is no limitation, as respects at least the subordinate standards of the church. I entirely dissent from the theory that there exists in the parliament of Canada, or in any court in this country, the right to say what is fundamental in doctrine and what is not. What in parliament would appear to one secular mind fundamental, would appear trifling to another. In a court of law it would be just the same. Those prerogatives are the prerogatives of the church. The church must have power to determine how and to what extent it exercises those prerogatives, a power unrestrained by any authority whether of parliament or of civil court.
The reason I contend that the power must be inherent is, first that it is impossible to suppress or direct the conduct of any church, in this respect. I put it in this way: if a churdh exercises the right, who is to say it nay? If a church exemnses it through the tribunal it creates to exercise it, who can say to such tribunal, nay? Who can dispute its power? It is said that in England the courts did so in 1994. The courts did not decide in England in 1904 that the church did not have the power. They decided that the church had not delegated to the assembly the power; because looking into the practices, records and precedents of the church, they found no case of its exercise, and no expression of its will such as would have empowered, the assembly. I am not going to argue whether, even on the ground stated by those judges, their decision was right or wrong. I have my opinion, but it is not pertinent whether they were right or wrong. The basis upon which the Lords of the Rrivy Council decided that there was not in the Assembly of the Free Church of Scotland the right to change its doctrine, is wholly absent in the case of the Presbyterian church in Canada. With all humility I express that opinion-because both textually and by precedent there has been evidence of the existence and of the exercise of such power throughout the history of the Canadian church. R is true that such exercise has been in cases where it could not very well be said-at leas: where I would not say-that there was any very fundamental or radical change. But 1

United Church of Canada
do not think this fact argues anything. I do not think indeed there is ever likely to be any very fundamental or radical change. The whole tradition, the constraint of tradition and the safeguards which tradition imposes, always protect a church against hasty or violent change. But if it wishes to	alter doctrine through	the
authority it creates for that purpose, thei there is no other authority to say it nay Consequently the church must have the power. The case decided in England in 1904 was decided on the conclusion of the judges, one and all, that, looking back at its practice and looking at the constitutional records of the Free Church, there was nothing to indicate that that church ever intended the General Assembly to exercise such a power. Looking into our practice and constitutional records in Canada, there is indication in both that euch intention has existed.
Referring to what is called the Blue Book, which is accepted certainly by the assembly, and I think we can say by the church, as constituting its code, sections 112 and 120, cannot be read in such a way as not to express both the inherent right of the church and the delegation of that right to the assembly, to restate or to alter doctrine. Section 112 contains the procedure for restating doctrine; but in the case of change section 120 applies, and provides an added safeguard ensuring tha: there cannot be, by the mere uncontrolled act of the assembly, a change of doctrine. There must be a reference back to the presbyteries, a series of bodies standing between the people and the assembly, and a confirmation of the change by a majority of these presbyteries, in order that it be effective. This safeguard is known as the Barrier Act. However, it does not really come into this argument. The point is that granted compliance with this Barrier Act whatever its terms, the authority to change exists.
Again I am confronted with the question, which I know is in the minds of many, was all this intended to apply to fundamental changes? I do not know where to draw the line, nor do I feel that we have any business to draw the line. It seems to me it is for the church to say what change is to be made great or small, and I feel that if parliament adopts any other principle we are launched upon a sea where the storms will be heavier and the dangers greater than those which surround us now.
_ I stated some moments ago that even were it true that the General Assembly in Canada was not so authorized-that is to say, even if 
it were arguable that our church, or rather the Presbyterian Assembly, does not, as it exists today, enjoy this power such a thing would mean only that the courts of Canada would decide as to the Presbyterian church, as the Lords of England decided as to the Free church. In this event it still seems to me it would be our duty to pass the bill. Why so? Let us look back over the history of the Free church case. As soon as it had been decided, a condition arose where the intervention of parliament became necessary. The condition was this: First that the church stripped of its membership to a very considerable degree, was deemed by parliament incapable of administering the trusts committed to it-I mean the trusts mainly of a property character- and the trustee being so incapable, the church having been forsaken by its members, save to the extent of a remnant, parliament was compelled to step in and take those trusts in large degree from that church, and repose (hem in another institution. Parliament as well by the same act of 1905 went on to declare that certain rights in relation to the alteration of doctrine were hereafter to be considered as existing in the Church of Scotland.
I do not need' to dwell on this act longer, but I come to the act of 1921. This was an act passed by the Imperial Llouse, which recited certain declaratory articles of faith of the Church of Scotland, declaratory articles which themselves affirmed the right of that church through its assembly to alter doctrine, and the parliament of Britain placed upon those articles the seal of legislation. The significance of this conduct of the British parliament is very great. It is very great when we remember the decision of the Lords in 1904. It shows that the parliament of England came to the conclusion that if, by reason of such judgment, there was imposed a restraint upon the power of the church through its assembly to alter its creed, such restraint should be removed; that it was not fit or right that the parliament of Britain should be in any position whereby it could superintend or censor alterations of doctrine made by the church itself.
Now let me at this point ask: Are we to go through any process, whether on the lines suggested by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) or on the lines now suggested by the Prime Minister, and as a result of one legal process or the other come after some length of time, to the conclusion, or rather have handed to us the conclusion of a court of law, that the Presbyterian Church of Canada through its assembly cannot alter doc-

United Church oj Canada
trine, as was the result in the case of the Free Church of Scotland? If so what then would be the attitude of parliament as respects the situation created? The Prime Minister says, "Well we could meet the situation Whatever it might be." I have to say immediately, our attitude necessarily towards any church in Canada in such circumstances would be the attitude which the British parliament took towards the Free Church of Scotland. If I have been entirely wrong in my contention as to what exists to-day and if the courts were to hold that the inherent right of change does not exist, could this parliament for a minute refuse an application from the Presbyterian church to be given that amplitude of power which became vested in 1921 in the Free Church of Scotland? I submit we could not. The Prime Minister brings in a condition that if a majority of the members of the church would come to us and ask for it, we would do it.

speechtext: I did not say a majority. I said if the constituted authorities of the church came and asked for it.

I am really very anxious
not to get into a controversy with the Prime Minister over this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend take my word for it at the moment, that that is what I meant?

Certainly. I notice he
said the majority-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Keep up the
controversy.

I am most anxious to
avoid a controversy only I noted it and I thought it was wrong. When the Prime Minister says "the authorities", I agree with him. If the recognized authorities of the church come and ask for it, we would do it. Very well, the recognized authorities of the Presbyterian church are now right at the doors of this parliament asking that we do this very thing. So I say, why throw the church into litigation even though we pay the costs of the litigation? Why prolong this controversy if it is bound to end after years of turmoil where it will end if we pass this legislation now? Why prolong the whole thing through tedious months or years, whether it be done by the litigation proposed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) or that proposed by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff)?
Let me, before I pass the subject, impress upon the committee, if I can, again, the
absolute necessity of our presuming from the beginning that we must concede to the church, whether it exists to-day or whether it does not, the full and unrestrained right to alter its creed. How are we to take a position which says to a church:	Bound as you are
by a regimen of doctrine, you must remain there no matter what your own courts may feel to be right in the light of advancing years. Though you, through your constituted courts, decide that you desire to modify this or modify that, you cannot do so. If you so alter, you are violating trusts, you are diverting to the teaching of other doctrines moneys or property committed to you for the propagation of the doctrine of your fathers. I am referring now particularly to the argument of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). Can we possibly assume for a day that sort of censorship over any church? Can we say to* a church: Though your majority desire a modification of doctrine, you cannot make such modification because it is diverting trust funds which you possess? If we say such thing we merely condemn that church to drift lifelessly on the reefs of time while its children abandon its altar and its creed. A majority goes first and then a majority of the remnant goes, until finally the church is left a shell. In this unhappy predicament we a parliament would be compelled, as was the parliament of Great Britain in the case of the Free Church, to invade the empty temple, disrobe the stranded church of its trusts and allocate them somewhere else. This course is the only alternative to conceding to every denomination its full right to alter doctrine and to have its trusts follow the destiny of the church itself. Between these ;wo courses will hon. gentlemen reflect which they would prefer to pursue-to hold the church within a strict regimen, the rigid restraints of any statement of doctrine which it had years before accepted and say that we must do such a thing because of trusts which that church has had under its care; or to hold that the church itself shall be the author and master of its creed and that its trusts will follow the destiny of the church? It is the latter course which I choose myself and that course I commend earnestly to parliament to-night.
I come now to the two amendments. I would prefer to oppose this bill direct, rather than to vote for either of the amendments suggested. I think it would be a more sensible treatment of those who come before this House. The amendment which is now part of the bill and which was inserted on motion of the hon. member for Lunenburg
United Church of Canada

provides that, in respect of certain litigation now launched in Ontario, any legislation which we pass shall not take effect until, as a consequence of this litigation, the courts finally declare that the assembly had power to enter into union upon the Basis of Union and the Appendix on Law. I take exception for this reason, that even if the defendants succeed, succeed right to the last court of appeal, there is no reason to be certain at all that there will be any judgment of the court on that question, yes or no. I call attention to the fact that this action is an action not between the General Assembly and the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs are not suing the General Assembly. They are suing a committee of the General Assembly, and the committee takes the ground in its defence that the pleading is not properly based, and does not constitute a cause of action at all. If the committee win on this ground, then of course there is no decision of the court as to what were the assembly's powers. In this event we would have the church committee winning against the plaintiffs and still no possibility of the legislation going into effect. The committee might win its case on almost any other ground but inasmuch as the assembly is not a party to the action at all, it is very doubtful if the courts would give any judgment as to what the powers of the assembly were.
Moreover, I think that these plaintiffs should have moved sooner and not waited until the eve of the opening of parliament. I think they were in a position to launch their action two years ago. It is true that they could give certain reasons for not doing so, for example, that they did not know the exact terms of this bill. But they knew all those things to which chiefly they take objection in the litigation. They knew that the church was negotiating for union on the Basis of Union and the Appendix on Law. Against this they direct their fundamental objection. They could have launched their litigation at that time, and their litigation then would have been on just as strong a footing as it can possibly be on to-day. Next, when they did commence about the middle of January, 1924, they asked for an injunction to restrain further proceedings towards securing the legislation. But we are now nearly four months in this session and there has been no application, no motion for an interlocutory injunction although such a step would have been the only way to take practical action to get the restraint. Application for interlocutory injunction was open to them, but they let the time go by and were content to hold the sword of
fMr. Meighen.]
litigation over this parliament. There is the further fact that the plaintiffs could absolutely defeat this law by simply dropping the action. For these reasons, I do not think we should be asked to abide the event of this lawsuit.
But again I emphasize: Above and beyond these arguments there stands the great dominating truth that no matter what the result of litigation, unless we are prepared to allow a condition to remain where a church is denied the right to change its doctrine, for that right alone is involved in the question of union, we would be certain to find ourselves back in just the position we are in to-day where we would be asked and bound to decide in the affirmative what we are asked to decide in the affirmative in this bill. I therefore look upon the amendment now under review as an evasion.
The Prime Minister has another motion pending	on the order paper to the
affect that this bill shall take effect only to the extent of the powers of parliament. Well, whether such motion passes or not I really do not care, because the result is exactly the same in either event; no bill takes effect beyond the powers of parliament. Parliament cannot do any more than it can do; so why inject mere surplusage into the body of this legislation?
Now, I want to discuss briefly the amendment suggested to-day,-though it is not technically before the House.-by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), an amendment to which the Prime Minister to-night gave his unqualified endorsement. I think this amendment is even more objectionable than the one embodied in the bill; and I am at -this advantage in discussing it, that its fatal features have been recognized already in the questions put by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) and by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). Let me read this amendment so that there be no question in the mind of any hon. member as to its words. The motion is that there be added to the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) these words:
Provided that as respects the Presbyterian Church in Canada, the provisions of this act shall apply only when all doubt has been removed as to the power of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, under its constitution and rules, to agree to a union of the Presbyterian Church in Canada with the Methodist and Congregational churches upon the basis of union as set out in schedule A of this act; provided, further, that this question shall be submitted for decision to the Supreme Court of Canada by a reference by the Minister of Justice.
My objections to this amendment are these: If the "stated case," as this is described by the Prime Minister, is made and the courts

United Church oj Canada
hold that there is no jurisdiction, what results? We have then a union effected by this parliament of the Methodist and Congregational churches, alone, a union which neither of them made at all and which neither of them wants, a union forced upon them against the expressed will of the recognized authorities of both churches. Does anyone dispute that this will be the outcome? Undoubtedly it will. Parliament has no right to do such a thing; and I venture to say that no hon. member comprehending the full meaning of this amendment will be likely to give it support. I come also to the objection suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I do not know who has advised the Prime Minister, and I do not want to pose as a great constitutional lawyer; but I say that this clearly is not a matter for a "stated case." There would be no difficulty in framing a " question " for the Supreme Court of Canada. This question could be put: "Had the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church power to negotiate for or to effect a union upon the terms of the Basis of Union and the Appendix on Law? The framing of this question would be simple and thus it could be put to the Supreme court. But that is not a stated case; a stated case involves the setting out of admitted facts. You cannot set out such facts because they are not admitted. On the other hand if you put the bald question-not a stated case at all, which is really intended by this amendment and what the Prime Minister himself has in mind-if you just put the bald question to the court, what is the court going to do about it? The court then has to get down and ascertain what are the facts upon which its judgment is to be based. These are in dispute, and there at once you have a law-suit. This subject I repeat is not appropriate for a stated case at all. One side will affirm, " Here is the Blue Book; this is the recognized authority, the discipline and law of the Presbj'terian church. Read what it says." The other side will say, " No, this Blue Book does not represent the law and the prophets of the Presbyterian church." Which side is right? The resultant is really a law-suit; it is not a stated case for the decision of the Supreme court. No matter how you go about to settle this matter in the courts, it is a law-suit, where the facts are in controversy and where you have two sides arranged in battle array against each other. Throughout all this controversy you will have two opposite contentions; you travel far over a long and stony road; you start in the
Supreme court and you land at length in the Privy Council before the law lords there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Where does my right hon. friend get that opinion?

I so interpret the suggested amendment, although the Prime Minister may interpret it differently:
Provided that as respects the Presbyterian Church in Canada, the provisions of this act shall apply only when all doubt has been removed as to the power of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada.
You do not remove "all doubt" on such a point until you have persevered to the last court. This is my interpretation of these words. The Prime Minister may have intended to stop at the Supreme Court of Canada but I do not think such is the legal effect of the amendment offered by the hon. member for Skeena.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would wish
to have it so worded at any rate.

Even so, it would only
mean that the path to be traversed would be a little shorter. It would be dangerous and expensive and finally inconclusive. For as a final word let me say that the end of the road in any event is exactly the end of the road indicated by the hon. member for Lunenburg. We land at the end of the one exactly where we do if we take the other course. If therefore as the final episode of either the one journey or the other the court finds that the power of the General Assembly does not exist; does any one fancy that the church will not return to parliament for that power? Does any one fancy that any church will be content to live under such a conscious disability? Will any church recognize the smallest assertion of authority in parliament as respects its own doctrine? No. Therefore why delay?-I had almost said why evade, but I wish to avoid every term that savours of offence. Why not rather face the real situation and end this matter now? Why not do now what undoubtedly in any event we will later on have to do, even according to the words of the Prime Minister himself, after months or years of confusion and estrangement, after all this litigation has been suffered and all this agony endured? I ask hon. members to consider the reasons I have advanced and to give them such weight as they feel to be their merit.
